title: PCOS / PCOD: Ayurvedic View, Diet & Lifestyle Care
excerpt: Irregular or missed periods, weight gain, acne and unwanted facial hair, difficulty conceiving — these are common signs of PCOS/PCOD. Learn what it is, how Ayurveda understands it, which tests are needed, what to eat and avoid, daily routine, safe home measures and when to see a doctor urgently.
content:
“My periods haven’t come for two or three months, my weight keeps rising and I’m getting pimples” — many teenage girls and young women say this today. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), PCOS affects an estimated 8–13% of women of reproductive age, and many of them do not even know they have it.

The good news is that with the right tests, a balanced diet, regular exercise and patient treatment, its symptoms can be managed to a large extent. This article is for information only — take any treatment only on the advice of your vaidya or doctor.

What is PCOS / PCOD?

PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome) is a hormone-related condition in which the ovary does not release an egg properly every month. Doctors usually diagnose it when at least two of these three are present:

  • Irregular ovulation — periods coming very late, very scanty, or not at all for months
  • Raised male hormones (androgens) — hair on the face and chin, acne, thinning scalp hair, or a high level in blood tests
  • Many small follicles on the ovaries on ultrasound — commonly called “cysts”

In India both names, PCOD and PCOS, are used; modern medicine mainly uses the term PCOS. Remember, these “cysts” are really partly developed follicles, not lumps or cancer. Before diagnosis, other causes such as thyroid or prolactin problems must be ruled out with tests, so do not draw conclusions yourself from an ultrasound alone.

The Ayurvedic View

The ancient Ayurvedic texts do not use the name “PCOS”, but they describe women’s diseases and disorders of artava (menstruation) in detail. Acharya Charaka explains that women’s genital disorders arise mainly from wrong diet and lifestyle and from vitiated artava:

विंशतिर्व्यापदो योनेर्निर्दिष्टा रोगसंग्रहे ।
मिथ्याचारेण ताः स्त्रीणां प्रदुष्टेनार्तवेन च ॥
— Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana 30

Meaning: In the compendium of diseases, twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract are described; in women they arise from improper diet and conduct (wrong eating habits and routine) and from vitiated artava.

From the Ayurvedic view, PCOS usually shows an imbalance of Kapha and Vata, weak agni (digestive fire), ama (undigested toxic residue) and increased meda (fat tissue). Together these block the artavavaha srotas (the channels related to menstruation), so the period does not come on time or comes very scantily. Some scholars compare it with artava-kshaya, nashtartava and the “Pushpaghni” state described in the Kashyapa Samhita. So the aim of treatment is to improve agni, reduce ama and excess meda, and bring Vata back to its proper direction.

Main Causes and Risk Factors

  • Family history of PCOS, diabetes or obesity
  • Insulin resistance — the body’s insulin not working properly, which affects both hormones and weight
  • Too much refined flour, sugar, sweets, cold drinks and junk food
  • Lack of exercise, sitting for long hours, sleeping during the day
  • Staying up late, screen addiction and irregular meal times
  • Constant stress, anxiety and lack of sleep

Symptoms and Tests

  • Irregular periods, coming more than 35 days apart or not coming for months
  • Sometimes very heavy or prolonged bleeding
  • Unwanted hair on the face, chin, chest or abdomen; acne and oily skin
  • Thinning or falling scalp hair
  • Weight gain, especially around the abdomen; dark, velvety skin on the neck or armpits
  • Difficulty conceiving, tiredness, irritability or low mood

For a correct diagnosis the doctor may advise a pelvic ultrasound, hormone tests (such as LH, FSH, testosterone), thyroid (TSH) and prolactin, fasting sugar or HbA1c, and cholesterol. If periods have stopped, a pregnancy test must be done first. PCOS can raise the later risk of diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, so keep getting checked from time to time.

Diet: What to Eat, What to Avoid

In PCOS the aim of diet is to keep blood sugar steady, improve agni and keep weight balanced. According to Ayurveda, light, fresh, warm food that reduces Kapha and meda is beneficial.

What to eat

  • Whole grains — barley, bajra (pearl millet), jowar, ragi, daliya, whole-wheat flour with bran (in limited amounts)
  • Pulses such as moong, masoor and chana, and sprouts — for protein
  • Green vegetables — bottle gourd, ridge gourd, bitter gourd, pointed gourd, fenugreek leaves, spinach, broccoli
  • Less-sweet fruits — guava, papaya, apple, pear, jamun (whole fruit, not juice)
  • A little flaxseed, sesame and walnut in meals; spices such as turmeric, cinnamon, fenugreek seeds and cumin
  • Lukewarm water, and thin buttermilk with lunch

What to avoid

  • Sugar, sweets, biscuits, cakes, cold drinks and packaged juices
  • Refined flour, noodles, pizza, burgers, chips and very fried food
  • Heavy, stale, very cold food and late-night meals
  • Constant snacking; eating even when not hungry

Daily Routine and Lifestyle

  • At least 30–45 minutes of brisk walking, cycling or other exercise every day — this is the most effective step in PCOS
  • If overweight, lose weight slowly; research shows that losing even 5–10% of body weight can improve periods
  • Sleep by 10–11 pm and wake early; avoid daytime sleep
  • Keep fixed meal times; a light dinner 2–3 hours before bed
  • Reduce stress with meditation, pranayama, music or time with family
  • Keep noting your period dates in a diary or on your phone — this information is very useful in treatment

Yoga

Surya Namaskar, Baddha Konasana (butterfly pose), Bhujangasana, Dhanurasana, Malasana, Kapalabhati, Anulom-Vilom and Bhramari pranayama are considered helpful. Caution: if pregnancy is possible, if bleeding is heavy during periods, or with high blood pressure or recent surgery, do Kapalabhati and difficult poses only after asking your doctor; learn yoga from a trained teacher.

Safe Home Measures

  • Fenugreek seeds: soaked overnight, a small amount with breakfast — considered helpful for sugar control
  • Cinnamon: a pinch in food or tea, as a spice — not in large amounts like a medicine
  • Lukewarm water and cumin-fennel water: for digestion and agni
  • Sunlight and sleep: walking in the morning sun and getting full sleep

Women taking diabetes medicines should not take large amounts of fenugreek or cinnamon — sugar may drop too low. These measures are only supportive; the main basis remains diet, exercise and regular check-ups.

Ayurvedic Treatment — With Caution

Ayurveda mentions many medicines for problems related to artava and meda, such as Shatapushpa (dill), Kanchanar Guggulu, Guduchi, Triphala, Ashoka, Lodhra and turmeric. After examination, when suitable, Panchakarma (such as Virechana or Basti) and Udvartana (massage with dry herbal powder) may be advised. However:

  • Which medicine or Panchakarma, in what amount and for how long — this is decided by the vaidya only after looking at the symptoms, test reports, constitution, pulse, age and plans for pregnancy.
  • Do not stop medicines prescribed by your doctor (such as hormone pills or metformin) on your own — make any change only after talking to your doctor.
  • Some herbs can change the effect of sugar or hormone medicines, so tell your vaidya the list of all your medicines; do not take “period-inducing” medicines yourself without tests.
  • If pregnancy is possible, during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and in teenage girls and older women, take any medicine only on the advice of a vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “PCOD cured from the root” or “guaranteed pregnancy”.

When to See a Doctor Urgently

  • Very heavy bleeding — soaking a pad every hour, dizziness or fainting — go to a hospital immediately
  • Periods have stopped with severe lower abdominal pain, or a positive pregnancy test
  • No period for three months or longer
  • Very rapid growth of unwanted hair, a deepening voice, or sudden heavy hair loss
  • Excessive thirst, frequent urination, or high sugar/BP reports
  • Long-lasting sadness, anxiety or thoughts of harming yourself — talk to someone close and a doctor right away

Summary — Points to Remember

  • PCOS is common and can be managed — don’t panic, get the right tests
  • Daily exercise and a little weight loss are the most effective steps
  • Less sugar, refined flour and junk food; more whole grains, pulses and vegetables
  • Sleep on time, reduce stress and note your period dates
  • Medicines and Panchakarma only under a qualified vaidya; don’t stop current medicines on your own
